state-to-state-purchases.story:
A government holds more than ownership of land. It holds sovereignty, the legal right to make and enforce law over a territory. For centuries rulers treated that right as something that could be sold, and this entry gathers the recorded sales. A sale of this kind is done by treaty. Once it is complete, the buyer's laws apply, and people's ordinary land titles may carry on underneath.

The list is long and goes back to the Middle Ages. Scotland paid Norway 4,000 marks sterling, plus a yearly 100 marks, for the Isle of Man and the Hebrides in 1266. The United States paid France $15 million for Louisiana in 1803, about $7 per square kilometre, and Russia $7.2 million for Alaska in 1867, about $4 per square kilometre. Brazil paid Bolivia £2 million for Acre in 1903. The United States paid Denmark $25 million for the 400 square kilometres of the Danish West Indies in 1916, or $62,500 per square kilometre, and in the same deal recognised Danish sovereignty over all of Greenland. In 1958 Pakistan bought the port of Gwadar from Muscat and Oman. Accounts of that price differ, with the list giving 5.5 billion Pakistani rupees and other accounts about £3 million. The last sale on the list came in 1963, when West Germany paid the Netherlands 280 million Deutsche Marks for Elten, Selfkant and Suderwick, 69 square kilometres in all. The prices are those of the time and are not adjusted for inflation. The list counts only transfers where money was paid for the territory itself, so it leaves out leases and payments for other purposes, such as war damages.

Every buyer and every seller on the list is a state or a ruler, and no private person or company appears. That matters to anyone who dreams of buying a piece of the world and running it. A private buyer can buy land and hold a deed, as anyone can, but the deed gives ownership under the seller's law. The seller's police, courts and tax office still apply. To get sovereignty a buyer would need other governments to accept that it now rules there, and the list shows no case of that happening for a private buyer.

Greenland shows how the idea survives and where it stops. In 2019 Donald Trump, then in his first term as US president, said he wanted the United States to buy Greenland, and the Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, called the idea absurd. He cancelled a planned state visit to Denmark on 20 August 2019. In his second term he returned to it, and Danish and Greenlandic leaders answered that Greenland is not for sale and that its people have the right to decide their own future. The Greenlandic government stated that it chooses the Danish Realm over the United States. On 21 January 2026, speaking at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Trump said he would not use force and would not impose the tariffs he had set for 1 February as pressure over Greenland. He said a framework for a future deal on Greenland and the Arctic had been formed, and he named Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the envoy Steve Witkoff to handle the talks. The right of a people to decide their own status has become part of how such a transfer is judged, which earlier sales ignored. No sale between states appears on that list after 1963.

add_sources.t: Trump rules out force, tariffs, says Greenland deal framework reached, Arctic Today, Jan 2026

state-to-state-purchases.why: The story called Gwadar (1958) the last sale, but its own listed source has Elten, Selfkant and Suderwick in 1963. The list prices Gwadar in rupees, so the conflict with £3 million is now stated. Added the January 2026 Davos statements and the 2019 cancelled visit.

swazi-concessions.story:
Eswatini, called Swaziland until 2018, is a small kingdom in southern Africa between what is now South Africa and Mozambique. Mbandzeni was its king from 1875 until he died in 1889. He had been chosen as a motherless boy, after the king-designate Ludvonga died in 1874. He inherited a strong army of more than 15,000 men and a practice of giving land rights to outsiders, since his father Mswati II had already granted land to Boers, Dutch-descended settlers, in the 1850s.

A concession is a grant of a right by a ruler, such as the right to graze cattle on a stretch of land, mine it, trade there or collect a fee. In Mbandzeni's time such papers became the way Swaziland was carved up. Concession seekers from Britain and from the Transvaal, the Boer republic next door, crowded into his capital at Mbekelweni, and the discovery of gold in the Transvaal brought more of them. The king and his officials were paid in gold, cattle or goods. 'Offy' Shepstone, a nephew of Sir Theophilus Shepstone, the administrator of the Natal colony, advised him, and more grants followed. Many of them overlapped, so that two people might hold rights to the same thing.

By one account, Boers tricked the king, who could not read or write, by having him mark papers with a cross after telling him the land concessions were not permanent, though the papers said they were. A ruler who cannot read the document is at the mercy of whoever explains it to him.

Mbandzeni tried to protect himself through alliances. In 1879 he sent about 10,000 soldiers to help the British defeat Sekhukhune, the Pedi king, and kept Zulu raids out of the Transvaal. Britain rewarded this by recognising Swaziland's independence and promising protection against Zulu and Boer encroachment. The concessions undid that promise. They gave the Boers and British a stake inside the country, and these interests were used at the conventions of 1884 and 1894, agreements between outside powers. No Swazi represented the kingdom directly at either negotiation. Shepstone spoke for Swazi interests in 1884 and Allister Miller in 1894. The border they drew with the South African Republic cut off many Swazi homes, including royal villages, which is why many Swazi people live in South Africa's Mpumalanga province today. The 1894 convention later made Swaziland a protectorate of that republic, meaning that it took charge of Swaziland's outside affairs.

Mbandzeni is quoted as saying on his deathbed that the Swazi kingship would die with him. A regency of about five years followed under Queen Tibati Nkambule, until his young son, Ngwane V, took the throne.

This entry belongs with purchases of territory because no single sale took place. Rights over the country passed in many small private grants, each of which looked like a limited business deal. Once enough foreign holders existed, their governments had a reason to step in, and sovereignty was settled above the king's head.
swazi-concessions.why: Added the length of the regency and the name of the successor.

tiran-sanafir.story:
Tiran and Sanafir are two uninhabited islands in the Red Sea at the entrance to the Gulf of Aqaba. Tiran covers about 80 square kilometres and is a popular place for divers. Its value is its position. It controls the narrow shipping lane that leads to Eilat in Israel and Aqaba in Jordan, and that lane is Israel's only way from the gulf to the Red Sea. Egypt closed it on 22 May 1967, and the closure was among the main causes of the Arab-Israeli war that year.

Who the islands belong to has long been argued. In 1949 and 1950, after Israeli forces reached the gulf, Egypt put troops on them with Saudi agreement, because Saudi Arabia had no navy to protect them. In 1954 Egypt told the UN Security Council that they had been sovereign Egyptian territory since a 1906 frontier deal with the Ottoman Empire. In 1957 Saudi Arabia asserted its own sovereignty in a memorandum to the UN. Israel seized the islands in the 1956 war, captured them again in 1967, and gave them back to Egypt under the 1979 peace treaty. Egyptian lawmakers said in 2017 that Saudi Arabia had asked for them back in 1984, 1989 and 1990.

In April 2016, during a visit to Cairo by the Saudi king, Egypt announced that it would hand them over. The Egyptian government said that the islands had always been Saudi and were only under Egyptian care. The announcement came alongside about $22 billion in agreements. Critics linked the deal to billions of dollars of Saudi aid to President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi's government and called it a sell-off of national land. The announcement set off the largest anti-government protests since he took office in 2014, and hundreds of people were arrested, most of whom were later released. Israel was told in writing weeks before the public announcement and gave its approval, because the change touched the military annex of its peace treaty with Egypt. Saudi Arabia said it would honour that treaty's terms for the islands.

The fight then moved through Egypt's institutions. In January 2017 the Supreme Administrative Court ruled against the transfer, and the lawyer Khalid Ali obtained court papers supporting Egyptian sovereignty. In April the Urgent Affairs Court set that ruling aside. The head of parliament, Ali Abdel Aal, said parliament would not recognise any ruling on the agreement. Supporters argued that ratifying treaties is parliament's right. On 13 June police beat several dozen protesters in downtown Cairo, and on 14 June parliament approved the deal by a vote in which supporters were asked to stand. A week later the Constitutional Court halted all rulings in the case, and Sisi ratified the treaty on 24 June. A government report said the agreement ended Egyptian sovereignty while Egypt kept administering the area for now, for the security of both countries.

Ratification did not finish the handover. In early 2018 the Egyptian outlet Mada Masr reported, citing an unnamed Western diplomat, that Saudi forces had replaced Egyptian troops on Tiran as a first step. Observers from the Multinational Force and Observers, the US-led group placed there to carry out the 1979 treaty, were also on the island. In July 2022 Israel approved the arrangement, and the United States announced that those observers would leave by the end of that year. They did not leave on that schedule. In December 2022 Axios reported that Sisi had halted the transfer. An analysis published in March 2023 by the Arab Center Washington DC said the matter was still unresolved. It gave a dispute over surveillance cameras meant to replace the observers as the technical reason and a disagreement over Saudi financial support for Egypt as the main one. Sources differ on where this stands now. That analysis treated sovereignty as still Egyptian until the transfer takes place, while Wikipedia lists Tiran under Saudi administration.

Whether this counts as a sale depends on who is describing it, since no price is stated in the treaty and aid is only what critics connect it to. It shows two things about moving territory today. A transfer between states can involve a third country whose treaties depend on the old arrangement. A government's own courts may object, and the outcome then depends on which institution has the last word.

add_sources.t: Al-Anani, Geopolitics of Small Islands: The Stalemate of Tiran and Sanafir's Transfer, Arab Center Washington DC, 29 Mar 2023
Western diplomat: Saudi troops stationed on Tiran Island, Mada Masr

tiran-sanafir.why: The story stopped at ratification in June 2017 and the entry was closed at 2017, but the handover was still unfinished in March 2023. Added the 2018 to 2023 events, the 1956 seizure and the $22 billion figure.

transylvania-purchase.story:
Before the American Revolution, the land west of the Appalachian Mountains was contested by several groups at once. The Royal Proclamation of 1763, issued by the British Crown after the French and Indian War, declared that land Indian Territory and forbade colonial settlement there. Settlers, traders and trappers kept going anyway. In the 1768 Treaty of Fort Stanwix, the Haudenosaunee, who claimed much of what is now Kentucky without living there, gave up their claim to Britain. The Shawnee and Cherokee, who actually used the land, were not consulted. The Shawnee fought Virginia in Lord Dunmore's War in 1774, lost, and gave up their claims south of the Ohio River. Virginia and North Carolina both also claimed parts of the area.

Into this came Richard Henderson, a North Carolina judge and land speculator. His Transylvania Company had a simple idea. If it bought the land directly from the Cherokee, it could perhaps get around the proclamation and win approval as a colony owned by its proprietors, as some early British colonies had been. Investors would profit by reselling land to settlers.

In March 1775, at Sycamore Shoals, most leading Cherokee chiefs, among them Attakullakulla and Oconostota, accepted a treaty selling a tract of about 20 million acres covering central and western Kentucky and part of north central Tennessee. The price was goods that some scholars estimate at about £10,000. The Cherokee leader Dragging Canoe refused to sign or obey the treaty. He moved to southeastern Tennessee, near Chattanooga, and his followers became known as the Chickamauga. Henderson hired the frontiersman Daniel Boone to cut the Wilderness Road through the Cumberland Gap so that buyers could get there. In May 1775 settlers agreed a written compact of government, a plan for running their own affairs.

Then the Revolutionary War began, and most settlement stopped except around the established towns. It also brought new governments that had every reason to reject him. The Virginia General Assembly cancelled the Kentucky claim in December 1778 and North Carolina cancelled the Tennessee part in 1783. Neither left him empty-handed. Each gave Henderson and his partners a grant of 200,000 acres, and Henderson, Kentucky, stands on the land he received along the Ohio River.

The legal lesson is about who gets to recognise a purchase. Henderson's deed came from people who lived on and used the land, yet the colonial governments applied their own rule, under which they alone could approve such a purchase, and they had claims of their own. So the deal gave him no title they would accept. The colony is described as extra-legal, meaning that it stood outside any law, and it existed only until someone with a government could rule on it. Its one lasting result was the compensation grant, which came from those same governments.
transylvania-purchase.why: Added the month, the acreage and the Cherokee refusal, which matters to a story about whether the sellers could convey the land.

trump-gaza.story:
Gaza is a small Palestinian coastal territory on the Mediterranean, devastated by war by early 2025. Hamas, a Palestinian armed group, had ruled it. On 9 February 2025, flying to the Super Bowl in New Orleans on Air Force One, US President Donald Trump told reporters, "I'm committed to buying and owning Gaza." He said other Middle Eastern states might rebuild sections of it under American auspices, and that the United States would make sure Hamas did not move back. He called the place "a demolition site" and had also spoken of permanently moving Palestinians out to create a "Riviera of the Middle East".

The remarks named no seller and no price. A purchase needs someone with the power to hand over the land and a sum agreed with them, and neither was described. Ezzat El Rashq of the Hamas political bureau answered that "Gaza is not a property to be sold and bought", called it part of occupied Palestinian land, and said that Palestinians would defeat any displacement plans.

Nothing was bought. US policy later took a different form. Trump's 20-point plan to end the war led to a US-backed Board of Peace, and in September 2026 that board proposed a six-month plan costing $2.45 billion, with 66 projects to begin rebuilding and governing Gaza. It estimated full reconstruction at about $35.2 billion in the medium term and another $71.4 billion over ten years. Its reported terms cover funded rebuilding and governance, with no American ownership or purchase. Hamas had not given up its weapons, and the Israeli military occupied about 60 percent of the territory.

The entry is here as a statement by a head of state that uses the language of a land deal for a place with a resident population and no party offering it for sale.

add_sources.t: Trump's Board of Peace proposes US$2.45B blueprint to begin Gaza reconstruction, CP24, 23 Sep 2026

trump-gaza.why: The story ended in February 2025. Added what followed, the Board of Peace plan of 2026, which is not a purchase.

eastern-greenland-case.story:
Greenland's far east coast is one of the emptiest places on Earth. It once had an Inuit population, but the last person was seen in 1823. By 1931 the stretch that this case concerns had no permanent population except for hunters and trappers at three main Norwegian stations, Jonsbu, Myggbukta and Antarctic Havn, and some smaller ones. Today it lies in Northeast Greenland National Park.

Norway and Denmark had shared this history. The medieval Norse colony in Greenland recognised the King of Norway, and Denmark and Norway were one kingdom from 1537 to 1814. When they separated, Denmark kept Greenland.

In June 1931 Hallvard Devold, a founder of the Norwegian Arctic Trading Company, raised the Norwegian flag at Myggbukta. On 10 July Norway issued a royal proclamation occupying the area and named it Erik the Red's Land, after the founder of the first Norse settlements in Greenland. Its legal theory was that this part of Greenland was terra nullius, Latin for land belonging to no one. Under old rules, a state can claim such land by actually occupying it. Norway argued that Denmark had never effectively done so.

Denmark went to the Permanent Court of International Justice, the world court of the time, two days later. It asked the court to declare the occupation unlawful and invalid. The case also turned on an earlier conversation. On 22 July 1919 Norway's foreign minister, Nils Ihlen, told the Danish minister that Danish sovereignty over all of Greenland would be met with no difficulties on the part of Norway, and Denmark treated that as binding.

On 5 April 1933 the court ruled for Denmark by twelve votes to two and found the proclamation unlawful and invalid. It did not accept Denmark's argument that Ihlen's words were an outright recognition of Danish sovereignty. It called them an unconditional and definitive promise, one that Wikipedia's account says became binding once later Norwegian statements corroborated it. Norway then gave up the claim.

The ruling teaches two rules that matter to anyone hoping to claim empty land. First, the amount of activity needed to hold a territory depends on the place. In a frozen, unpopulated region, a state can own it with little presence, as long as it has shown that it means to rule and has acted accordingly. So a settler who finds a coast with no government on it cannot assume it is free. Second, a foreign minister's spoken promise can bind a state. Private stations and a later flag could not outweigh Denmark's prior authority.
eastern-greenland-case.why: The ruling was overstated by implication: the court rejected the reading of the Ihlen statement as recognition and treated it as a promise. Added the exact date. The PCIJ text itself could not be opened.

hans-island.story:
Hans Island, called Tartupaluk in Greenlandic, is a bare, uninhabited rock of 1.3 square kilometres in Nares Strait, the narrow sea between Canada's Ellesmere Island and Greenland. Greenland is a self-governing part of the Kingdom of Denmark, so the dispute over it was between Canada and Denmark. It is a useful case because it shows how two friendly states handled a small rock that neither would give up.

In 1973 the two countries signed a treaty fixing their sea boundary through the strait, and the line deliberately stopped either side of the island because they could not agree who owned it. Canada said the island came with the 1880 transfer of the Hudson's Bay Company's lands to Canada. Denmark said it was part of Greenland and had been used by Greenlandic Inuit for hunting, and pointed to its geology and to the 1933 world court ruling on Greenland. The name comes from Hans Hendrik, the Greenlandic helper of the American explorer Elisha Kent Kane, whose account of an expedition of 1853 describes naming the rock after him. Neither side took the question to an international court.

What followed became known as the Whisky War. Visitors from each side left flags and bottles of drink for the other. In March 2004 Canadian newspapers reported that Danish warships and sailors had gone to the island. On 20 July 2005 Canada's defence minister, Bill Graham, visited and raised a flag, and five days later Denmark said it would complain about the unannounced visit. NPR reported a summer of flag-planting and gift-leaving. No one was hurt, and the two countries are NATO allies.

On 14 June 2022 the foreign ministers Mélanie Joly of Canada and Jeppe Kofod of Denmark, with Greenland's premier Múte Egede, settled it. The agreement split the island along a natural ridge. Accounts of the shares differ, with some giving roughly 60 percent to Denmark and the rest to Canada and Wikipedia saying nearly in half. This gave the two countries their first land border, 1,280 metres long. The Danish parliament ratified the agreement on 19 December 2023. It also settled their remaining sea boundary in the Lincoln and Labrador seas. The ministers exchanged bottles of Canadian Sortilège whisky and Danish Gammel Dansk bitter.

Nobody from outside could have stepped in and claimed the rock during those 49 years. Being disputed did not make it free, since both states already claimed it. The case shows the reverse of the micronation idea, in which a gap between claims creates an opening. Here the gap closed by agreement between the two states.
hans-island.why: The 1853 expedition was American, under Kane, with a Greenlandic helper, not 'with Danish participation'. The warship reports date from 2004 and came before the 2005 visit. Noted the conflict over shares and added the ratification and border length.

difc-lcia-abolition.story:
The DIFC-LCIA Arbitration Centre was an arbitration institution in the Dubai International Financial Centre, the separate common-law zone in Dubai. Its name joined the zone with the London Court of International Arbitration, an established English institution.

Decree No. 34 of 2021, effective 20 September 2021, abolished it. Its rights and obligations passed to the Dubai International Arbitration Centre, known as DIAC. Agreements made before that date were deemed valid, and DIAC administers disputes under them unless the parties agree otherwise. Contracts that had named the old centre were suddenly left to work out what they meant.

Courts have since read the decree so as to keep the bargain. In Narciso v Nash (ARB 009/2024), the DIFC Court of First Instance, through Justice Michael Black KC, granted an interim order on 20 May 2024 stopping a party from pursuing proceedings in Sharjah, and on 20 June 2024 it gave its reasons and kept the order in place until the claim for a permanent order is decided. It held that a seat in the DIFC implies the DIFC courts as supervisors, that the decree did not void the agreement, and that the parties could use DIAC or another centre.

This is a useful case for anyone relying on private courts inside a state's zone. The arrangement gave real, enforceable justice to many parties, and one decree could still rearrange its institutions. The agreements survived because courts in that same system chose to preserve them.
difc-lcia-abolition.why: The order is interim; the wording read as final.

prospera-arbitration-center.story:
The Próspera zone on Roatán, Honduras, built its justice system on arbitration. Article 20 of Honduras's zone law said zones should use binding arbitration for all matters involving contracts or property. Próspera's charter let its default provider set up original and appeal tribunals for causes of action arising within the zone. Residents sign an Agreement of Coexistence, which appears to be the residency contract the statute refers to, and it includes arbitration by default. The zone and its related bodies also make a standing offer to arbitrate disputes with anyone, which appears to remove the need for a separate agreement in such cases. The practitioners who describe it caution that this covers disputes involving the zone's own organs more than purely private commercial disputes.

The default provider is the Próspera Arbitration Center, a Texas limited liability company. It publishes rules for small claims, evictions, labour and hazardous activity, and it files cases electronically. There are two tracks. The private track is confidential and needs the parties' agreement and a privacy surcharge. The public track looks much like a court, starting with a complaint and summons, and its decisions on zone law are meant to be published and binding as precedents. Practitioners writing about it said they had not found a public database of such awards.

They also noted that Honduras is a party to the New York Convention, and that the public track may raise questions about consent before a foreign court. Arbitration here reaches people who may not have signed a specific clause, which is the opposite of how arbitration normally gets its force. Honduras's Supreme Court declared the zone laws unconstitutional on 20 September 2024. The Honduran state argues that the ruling applies from the start, as if the laws had never been valid. Honduras Próspera Inc. has a claim against Honduras before ICSID, the World Bank's investment arbitration centre, arguing that ending the zone regime violated its investment rights and promised legal stability. In October 2025 the Honduran state's attorney general said the claim had fallen from about $10.8 billion to $1.63 billion. How the ruling affects awards from this centre has not been decided by any reported ruling, and the zone continues to operate.

add_sources.t: Próspera ZEDE redujo 85% el monto reclamado en arbitraje contra Honduras, Revista E&N, 23 Oct 2025

prospera-arbitration-center.why: The standing offer was stated too broadly. Added the exact ruling date, the Honduran state's ex tunc position and the ICSID claim.

sealand-sale-attempts.story:
Sealand has been offered for sale more than once, and each episode shows what buying it could and could not bring. Sealand is a Second World War sea fort on two concrete legs, about 6 nautical miles off Suffolk, which the Bates family has called an independent principality since 1967. The first episode went badly for the family. In 1978 Alexander Achenbach, a German who described himself as Sealand's prime minister, invited Roy and Joan Bates to Austria to discuss a sale.

While they were away, in August, his hired men took over the fort and held their son Michael hostage. The Bates family retook it by helicopter and held Achenbach's lawyer for about six weeks. In January 2007 The Pirate Bay, a website that indexes file-sharing links, tried to buy Sealand after harsher copyright measures in Sweden pushed it to look for a base elsewhere. Between 2007 and 2010 Sealand was offered for sale through a Spanish estate company, InmoNaranja, at an asking price of €750 million, then about £600 million.

No sale was completed. The legal background made any sale an unusual one. Since 1 October 1987 the fort has stood inside Britain's 12-mile territorial sea. A court in Cologne held in 1978 that Sealand has no real territory, population or effective government, and no state recognises it. A buyer could at most have received possession of the structure and the family's claims. Britain's inaction so far has concerned one family doing little harm. It is reasonable to expect a different response to a file-sharing site accused of breaching copyright, though no court or government decided that, because the sale never happened.

HavenCo's experience on the same fort between 2000 and 2008 suggests the same limit, since a data-hosting firm that relied on the location for protection from courts could not keep customers or the site. Roy Bates died in 2012 and his son Michael took over, and the family continues to sell titles rather than the fort.
sealand-sale-attempts.why: Added the month and the hostage-taking.

asteroid-redirect-mission.story:
The Asteroid Redirect Mission was a NASA proposal of 2013. A robotic spacecraft would rendezvous with a large near-Earth asteroid, use grippers and a drill to take a boulder of about 4 metres, and carry it to a stable orbit around the Moon. Astronauts on an Orion capsule would later visit it, possibly in 2026, and the mission would also test ways of deflecting an asteroid to protect Earth.

An earlier version looked at bringing back a whole small asteroid, and a feasibility study from the Keck Institute for Space Studies had looked at that in 2012. If funded, it would have launched in December 2021. The proposed 2018 budget called for its cancellation, it received notice of defunding in April 2017, and NASA announced the close-out on 13 June 2017. Its ion thruster work continued, and NASA planned to use that electric propulsion on the Lunar Gateway's Power and Propulsion Element.

The mission is the nearest thing to a plan to move part of a celestial body. It would have been a government project, under US jurisdiction, and the question of what a moved boulder is under space law never had to be answered. Article II of the Outer Space Treaty bars appropriation of celestial bodies by claim, use or occupation. Article VIII speaks of objects launched or constructed, and a boulder is neither.

The US law of 2015 lets American citizens own asteroid resources they recover, without saying how large a resource can be. Because the mission never flew, no court or government had to decide whether a moved boulder is a resource, a body or a new object.
asteroid-redirect-mission.why: Added what became of the thruster work. Reworded a loose claim about what is known so that it says why the question stayed open.

innovation-zones-nevada.story:
Innovation Zones were a 2021 proposal to let technology companies form a new kind of local government in Nevada. The main backer was Blockchains, Inc., which owned about 67,000 acres in and around the Tahoe Reno Industrial Center in Storey County east of Reno. It wanted to break away from the county government and build a smart city, with plans for about 36,000 residents over time. Storey County's population was about 4,000.

Governor Steve Sisolak announced the idea in his State of the State address. The company had given $10,000 to his 2018 campaign and $50,000 to a political committee linked to him. Critics said the plan would allow company towns. Storey County raised logistical and money concerns, and there were questions about where the water would come from. That spring the governor stepped back after he could not persuade lawmakers, and the legislature passed a bill to study the concept. A special committee met twice from August.

About a week before 7 October 2021 the chief executive, Jeff Berns, wrote to the governor withdrawing the request and complaining that the plan had found no champion. He said the company had spent more than $300 million in Nevada and would no longer build a mixed-use city at Painted Rock, though it still planned a technology park. No Innovation Zone was ever created, and no court considered the idea. The case shows the first obstacle to a company district, which is the vote of a legislature, reached before any legal question arises.
innovation-zones-nevada.why: The letter was sent the week before the 7 October report, so it may predate October.

reedy-creek-district.story:
Reedy Creek was a Florida local government built around Walt Disney World. Walt Disney flew over the Orlando area in November 1963, and shell companies then bought land cheaply. In 1966 Disney subsidiaries asked a court to create a drainage district, and on 12 May 1967 Governor Claude Kirk signed the Reedy Creek Improvement Act, which made the district and two cities, one of which was renamed Lake Buena Vista around 1970. A planned living community called EPCOT was the main argument for these powers, and it was never built as a working city.

The district ran land use, building codes, drainage, utilities, roads, fire protection and emergency services. Votes went by land, one per acre, so Disney in effect chose the board, and each supervisor held a five-acre lot. The Florida Supreme Court held in 1968 that the Act did not break the state constitution.

The end came through politics. After Disney opposed a state education law in 2022, the legislature voted to dissolve independent districts formed before November 1968, effective June 2023. Critics noted more than $1 billion in district bonds. In February 2023 the state instead kept the district, renamed it the Central Florida Tourism Oversight District, and gave the governor the appointment of its board, subject to Senate confirmation. The old board had just signed a development agreement limiting the new board. Disney sued the governor and lost in federal court on 31 January 2024, then appealed. On 27 March 2024 it settled the state suits and put the federal appeal on hold while a new development agreement was negotiated. The settlement followed the governor's replacing two Disney critics on the board with two Disney supporters. The land stayed Disney's and the government passed to the state's appointees.
reedy-creek-district.why: Added the appeal, the exact dates and the terms of the settlement.

vernon-california.story:
Vernon is a city of about five square miles next to Los Angeles, incorporated on 22 September 1905 to promote industry along the railways and later known as exclusively industrial. It added industrial land by annexation while leaving out homes, and in 1932 it voted bonds for its own power plant, and cheap electricity drew large factories. Its population fell from 1,269 in 1930 to about 90 in 1980. The city owned nearly all the housing, and tenants were mostly city workers or people linked to them, paying very low rents. It has fewer than 90 voters by one account, and it reported about 46,000 jobs.

The result was a small electorate that depended on the city for its homes. A firefighter who tried to run for mayor in 1979 was reportedly evicted. In 2006 newcomers moved into a converted office building to contest the council. The city cut off their power and tried to evict them, a judge let them run, and they lost by a landslide. That November charges were filed against the mayor, Leonis Malburg, and others. He was found guilty of fraud in 2010 and ordered to pay more than $500,000. A former administrator, Bruce Malkenhorst, pleaded guilty in May 2011 to misusing public money, was fined and kept a large pension.

In 2011 Assemblyman John Pérez backed a bill to dissolve cities with under 150 residents, which meant only Vernon. The Assembly passed it 58 to 7. Vernon agreed to reforms and to set aside $60 million for nearby cities, and the state Senate rejected the bill on 29 August 2011. New apartments opened to the public in 2015, and the population reached 222 in 2020.
vernon-california.mechanism: A small city controlled through ownership of nearly all the housing
vernon-california.why: The mechanism called Vernon a general-law city, yet its own source refers to the city's charter, and it said 'all' where the story says 'nearly all'. Added the outcomes for Malburg and Malkenhorst.

marshall-islands-dao-act.story:
The Marshall Islands is an independent Pacific country in free association with the United States. It has a history of offering legal products to the world, including a ship register started in 1988. In 2022 it passed a Decentralized Autonomous Organization Act giving blockchain-run groups a legal form, and a further Act in 2023 built on it. It is described as the first sovereign state to recognise such groups as their own kind of legal entity.

This differs from the US state laws in one way that matters for this subject. The law comes from a member of the United Nations, so a DAO registered there is a legal person of a sovereign state. According to a legal commentary published in November 2023, the 2022 law allowed near-complete anonymity for members, requiring only one person to give know-your-customer details to the registry. The 2023 Act allows series DAOs, where sub-DAOs hold separate assets and liabilities, and it allocates legal risk to the DAO instead of the participants. It also shields DAOs from responsibility for the open-source software they create. A company called MIDAO Directory Services acts as the registrar's office.

Whether courts elsewhere will respect this shield when local people bring claims against a nearly anonymous group has not been decided. The nearest US ruling points to the risk. On 18 November 2024 Judge Vince Chhabria of the federal court in northern California, in a suit by a token holder, Andrew Samuels, held that Lido DAO operates as a general partnership, so that its decentralised governance did not shield it from partnership law. Partners in such a firm can be personally liable, and the claims were allowed to proceed, with no final judgment reported. That ruling did not concern a Marshall Islands registration, so it does not answer the question for a DAO that holds one. The law gives a DAO a home and gives it no authority over land, passports or people.

add_sources.t: Samuels v. Lido DAO report, CryptoSlate, Nov 2024

marshall-islands-dao-act.why: 'Not tested' left out the closest real ruling, Samuels v. Lido DAO (N.D. Cal. 2024). Added it and said why it does not settle the point.

utah-dao-act.story:
Utah's act was signed on 13 March 2023 and took effect on 1 January 2024. Where Wyoming fitted DAOs into its company law, Utah made a distinct legal entity, the limited liability decentralised autonomous organisation, or LLD. Its authors adapted a model law written by a group called the Coalition of Automated Legal Applications.

An LLD exists as a set of rules encoded on a permissionless blockchain in one or more smart contracts. It may have different classes of members and must be formed by at least one natural person, called a disclosed incorporator. Unlike ordinary small companies, which need not submit their bylaws, an LLD must show the Utah Division of Corporations evidence that its code has undergone quality assurance, and it must provide a public interface for monitoring all its transactions.

Members are liable only for their on-chain contributions, and they are not liable for the acts of other members or for debts beyond the LLD's assets. There is one exception. Members who vote for the LLD to refuse a court-ordered remedy may be personally liable in proportion to their governance rights. So the statute that offers the most protection to a software-run group also makes a court's order the point where the protection stops. It gives a community its nearest thing to a constitutional form in US law, and it places that form under the courts of the state.
utah-dao-act.why: Removed a characterising word. The dates and rules matched the source.

wyoming-dao-law.story:
In 2021 Wyoming became the first US state to explicitly recognise the legal status of decentralised autonomous organisations, groups that make decisions through software on a blockchain. The act, SEA No. 73, let a DAO register as a new type of limited liability company, the common business form that protects owners' personal assets from the firm's debts. It added a supplement to the state's company law, with rules on formation, articles of organisation, operating agreements, smart contracts, management, voting rights, withdrawal of members and dissolution.

The legislature amended it in 2022 through SEA No. 16. A DAO may now be managed by its members or by an algorithm to varying degrees. The Secretary of State may dissolve a DAO within 30 days of formation if a publicly available identifier is not provided in its filing. The law also set out a way to petition a court for dissolution.

Wyoming's law gave CityDAO the form it used to buy 40 acres near Cody. The law is a company statute and gives no government powers. A DAO company stands where any other company stands under state law, with county zoning, state courts and federal law applying as usual. Its value is in giving a blockchain group a name that can sign a deed and in protecting members from being treated as partners. That risk is real for groups that lack such a form. On 18 November 2024 a federal judge in northern California, in a suit by a token holder against Lido DAO, held that Lido DAO operates as a general partnership, and the claims were allowed to proceed. Legislators elsewhere have looked to it, and Utah, New Hampshire and others later considered different forms.

add_sources.t: Samuels v. Lido DAO report, CryptoSlate, Nov 2024

wyoming-dao-law.why: Added the Lido DAO ruling, which shows what the company form is meant to avoid.

falepili-union.story:
On 9 November 2023 Tuvalu and Australia signed a treaty called the Falepili Union, and it entered into force on 28 August 2024. Falepili is a Tuvaluan word for good neighbourliness, care and mutual respect. The treaty covers migration, climate change and security.

Australia promised three main things. It would provide permanent residency for up to 280 Tuvaluans a year, a pathway meant to allow movement with dignity. It would help Tuvalu in the event of a major natural disaster, a public health emergency of international concern, or military aggression. And it would recognise Tuvalu's future statehood and sovereignty despite sea-level rise. Prime Minister Feleti Teo described this as the first time a country had committed legally to recognise Tuvalu's future statehood. He said he would seek the same assurance from more countries.

In return Tuvalu agreed to engage with Australia before any partnership, arrangement or engagement with another state or body on security matters. Such arrangements must be mutually agreed by both countries, and the two agreed to resolve disputes between themselves without any court or third party. This caused debate. Former Prime Minister Enele Sopoaga said it would undermine sovereignty and vowed to repeal it. Teo said he wanted to revisit the mutual agreement requirement and later said he wanted arrangements that stop short of revising the treaty. Australia tabled the treaty for ratification on 26 March 2024, after the new government confirmed it wanted to proceed, and on 16 October 2024 it handed Tuvalu a Guardian-class patrol boat.

It is the clearest case of a state buying legal assurance about its future existence by treaty. It binds only Australia and Tuvalu. It also shows the usual trade, since a small state gained protection and migration rights and gave up some freedom of action.
falepili-union.why: The security clause was described too weakly: both countries must mutually agree. Added the tabling and the patrol boat handover.

roger-ver-expatriation.story:
Roger Ver is an early Bitcoin investor who describes himself as a libertarian and anarcho-capitalist. His case shows what happens when one of the most practised versions of flag theory meets the state the person left.

Ver obtained citizenship of Saint Kitts and Nevis, a Caribbean country that sells citizenship through an investment programme, and in 2014 he gave up his United States citizenship. An Ars Technica headline in January 2015 reported that he could not then get back into the United States. He has lived in several countries, including Japan and Antigua, and he obtained citizenship of Antigua and Barbuda in 2020.

In April 2024 he was arrested in Spain on a US indictment alleging tax evasion. The charges were tax charges, and the US government treated him as a fugitive until a deal was struck. He disputed them, moved to dismiss them, and hired lawyers with close ties to Donald Trump, along with Roger Stone as a lobbyist. On 14 October 2025 he entered a deferred prosecution agreement with the US Department of Justice and agreed to pay $49.9 million. Under such an agreement the charges are put aside if the terms are met, so the case did not end in a conviction, and the government later dismissed the indictment.

Two things stand out for anyone thinking about this route. Giving up a nationality did not end the tax claims of the country he had left. A second passport also did not stop an arrest in a third country that has its own extradition arrangements with the United States.
roger-ver-expatriation.why: Added his status as a fugitive before the agreement.

peanut-hole-okhotsk.story:
The Peanut Hole is a strip of international water in the middle of the Sea of Okhotsk, about 55 kilometres wide and 480 kilometres long. It lies more than 200 nautical miles from any coast, so it falls outside the exclusive economic zone of Russia, which surrounds it. That makes it high seas, open to ships of all countries, in the middle of a sea otherwise under one country's resource control.

Its name became known through fishing. Because any country could fish there, many did in 1991, and by 1992 they had taken perhaps as much as one million metric tons of pollock. Russia saw this as a threat, since the fish move between the pocket and its zone. In 1993 China, Japan, Poland, Russia and South Korea agreed to stop fishing there until stocks recovered, although they did not agree on what would follow. The UN Straddling Fish Stocks Agreement, in effect since 2001, later set a framework for countries to manage together fish that move between a coastal zone and the high seas.

The seabed then took a different path from the water. Russia argued to the UN Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf that the sea floor there is part of its continental shelf. A subcommittee accepted this in November 2013, and in March 2014 the full commission issued recommendations in Russia's favour. Since then the seabed and subsoil have been treated as part of Russia's shelf, while the water remains high seas.

This shows how the law of the sea can split a place in two. A ship may sail there under its own flag as on any open ocean. Anything fixed to the bottom meets Article 80 of UNCLOS, which gives the coastal state control over artificial islands and certain structures on its shelf. A founder who saw an empty pocket of high seas on a map would find, on looking closer, that Russia holds exclusive rights over the seabed's resources and over structures fixed to it, and that the same state's zone surrounds the pocket on all sides.
peanut-hole-okhotsk.why: The commission issues recommendations and does not give court rulings. Added the 2001 fish stocks agreement.

otrag.story:
OTRAG was a West German company founded in 1974 by Lutz Kayser and based in Stuttgart. It is often described as the first commercial developer of space launch vehicles. Its idea was a rocket built from large numbers of identical mass-produced units, each made of tank tubes with a simple engine. Using kerosene and nitric acid and no pumps, it aimed for a launch cost about one tenth of conventional rockets, carrying satellites of one to ten tons or more.

It did its flight testing abroad. Its first flight was on 18 May 1977 at Shaba North, in what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo. France and the Soviet Union opposed German long-range rocket work, and under their pressure the Zairian government closed the site in 1979. The West German government then cancelled the project and closed the company's operations in Germany. OTRAG moved to Seba Oasis in Libya in 1980 and tested there from March 1981 to December 1982. Its small four-unit rockets, 6 and 12 metres long, mostly reached heights of 20 to 50 kilometres, and the highest figure in the launch list, 150 kilometres, is marked as uncertain. Some had guidance or component failures. The company's last launch came on 19 September 1983 at Esrange in Sweden.

It left Libya in 1987, when it shut down. Muammar Gaddafi's government confiscated all of its equipment and installations there, and its German investors lost their money. None of its 18 recorded launches reached orbit, and a full orbital vehicle was never assembled. The case is the nearest example of a private rocket firm seeking room in a weak or distant host state. It shows how much such a firm then depends on one government. Moving test sites from one country to another was possible, but each move ended when a government acted. Foreign pressure closed the site in Zaire, West Germany shut the operations at home, and Libya kept the equipment.
otrag.why: 'Kept its base in West Germany the whole time' was wrong: Bonn closed its German operations after 1979. 'Some' equipment was in fact all of it. Added the missing reason for leaving Zaire and the investors' loss.

baikonur-lease.story:
Baikonur is a launch site in Kazakhstan run by Russia. The Soviet Union founded it as a test range in 1955 for its first intercontinental missile, and it became the base of the Soviet space programme. All Russian crewed flights leave from there. In 1991 the Soviet Union broke up and the site found itself in the new state of Kazakhstan. Russia wanted a 99-year lease.

It agreed to pay US$115 million a year for 20 years with an option for a 10-year extension. In 2005 Russia's upper house ratified an agreement extending the lease to 2050 with the rent fixed at the same figure, and the rent has been a long-running source of dispute. Sovereignty stayed with Kazakhstan. Under Article VII of the Outer Space Treaty, a state whose territory is used for a launch is liable along with the one that launches, so each launch involves both countries, and agreements between them can divide the cost.

The site also shows who bears the local burden. Spent stages fall on the ground downrange, and local people salvage them. Researchers have reported harm to the environment and to health from UDMH, a highly toxic rocket fuel. The host has also used its position. In March 2023 Kazakhstan seized the Baiterek launch complex over a reported $29.7 million debt owed by Russia. Part of the site, Gagarin's Start, made its last launch on 25 September 2019, and in 2023 the two countries announced plans to turn it into a museum. On 27 November 2025 the launch of Soyuz MS-28 significantly damaged the pad at Site 31/6, and Roscosmos announced its restoration on 3 March 2026. A private group could hope to copy the form of this arrangement. It is the strongest example of a launch site leased across a border, and it rests on a superpower's earlier investment. No private lessee has obtained anything comparable.
baikonur-lease.why: Added the 2005 ratification, the 2023 Baiterek seizure, and the 2025 pad damage and repair.

malindi-san-marco-platform.story:
The Luigi Broglio Malindi Space Center is a retrofitted oil rig off the coast of Kenya, run by Italy's space programme. It grew out of a 1962 agreement between the University of Rome and NASA, and the Italian Space Agency has managed it since 2004. A sister platform, Santa Rita, hosted launches in 1964. The first launch from the main San Marco platform was a Scout rocket on 26 April 1967, and the last was on 25 March 1988. That record makes it one of the earliest offshore launch sites and an early case of one country's space programme operating off another country's coast. A site close to the equator gives a rocket extra speed from the Earth's spin, and a platform at sea keeps launches away from towns.

The platforms fell into disrepair in the 1990s, while a ground station on the cape stayed in use for tracking satellites. Italy has announced plans to reopen the launch site after a gap of nearly 40 years. Kenya has joined the Outer Space Treaty and the Liability Convention, according to the UN's table of 1 January 2026, and it has not joined the Registration Convention or the Rescue Agreement. Italy launches and procures, so it counts as a launching state. Reading the text, a launch from Kenyan territory would also make Kenya a launching state under the treaty's words "territory or facility", and the two countries could agree how to divide any cost between them, as the UN recommended in 2004.

The platform shows what a real sea launch looks like when it runs by agreement between two governments. Founders hoping for a site with no state behind it can draw little from it, since every part of its operation has rested on one state's programme and another state's consent.
malindi-san-marco-platform.why: The entry had no dates. 'Will reopen' was firmer than the source, which says plans and 'may soon'. Added the history and the state of the site.

marino-garcia-four-roses.story:
United States v. Marino-Garcia is a 1982 decision of the US Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit, joined with a second case, United States v. Cassalins-Guzman. It is the usual starting point in American law for what a country may do to a stateless vessel. The Coast Guard cutter Dependable approached the Four Roses on the high seas about 65 miles off the west coast of Cuba and 300 miles from Florida.

She carried about 57,000 pounds of marijuana and nine foreign crewmen, and nothing showed the cargo was meant for the United States. The court treated her as stateless. She appeared to be registered in Honduras under the name Jenny Conner, but when stopped she flew no flag and showed no Honduran markings, her name had been altered, and "Miami, Florida" was stencilled on her bow. In the second case the cutter Lipan found the Lady Mark near Cuba with about 20,000 pounds of marijuana and four national flags aboard. Her crew said she was registered in Colombia.

The trial judge had dismissed that indictment because nothing linked the vessel to the United States. The appeals court upheld the first convictions, in which seven men had received five-year sentences and two had received seven years, and it reversed the dismissal. It held that American drug law reached stateless vessels on the high seas and that international law permitted this with no connection to the United States. It called such vessels "international pariahs" with no internationally recognised right to navigate the high seas, and "floating sanctuaries from authority".

It said commentators had unanimously agreed that all nations may assert jurisdiction over them. That statement is less secure today. Writers now divide between an "any state" view and a "nexus" view, and some argue that the right to board does not bring a right to prosecute. The case binds courts in one part of the United States, and no international court has endorsed it.
marino-garcia-four-roses.why: 'Once been registered' was not what the opinion says. Added the vessel's former name, the Colombia claim and the sentences.

chinese-taipei-formula.story:
Taiwan's government lost China's seat at the United Nations in 1971, and today only a small number of states recognise it. It still takes part in many international bodies under names worked out for the purpose. The best known is Chinese Taipei.

The Olympic dispute shows how this came about. The International Olympic Committee recognised both the mainland and the Taiwan-based committees in 1954. The People's Republic withdrew in 1958 in protest. At the 1976 Games in Montreal, the host government of Canada refused to let the Republic of China team use that name, and the team withdrew a day before the opening ceremony. In April 1979, at its session in Montevideo, the IOC recognised the People's Republic's committee, and the Nagoya Resolution of that year set out a name for the Taiwan-based committee. The deal was completed by the Lausanne Agreement, signed on 23 March 1981 by the IOC's president, Juan Antonio Samaranch, and the Taiwan-based committee's president, Shen Chia-ming, which fixed its name, flag and emblem and put it on an equal footing with other national committees. Under this arrangement its athletes could keep competing, without their national name, anthem or flag. In 1989 the two Olympic committees agreed in Hong Kong on how the name is written in Chinese at events held in China.

The same approach spread elsewhere. Taiwan is a member economy of APEC, the Pacific trade forum, as Chinese Taipei, and it belongs to the World Trade Organization as the Separate Customs Territory of Taiwan, Penghu, Kinmen and Matsu. Many in Taiwan find the term humiliating and there have been campaigns to change it. In a 2018 referendum voters rejected a proposal to change the Olympic name to Taiwan.

The case shows that a place with no general recognition can sit in functional bodies if their rules allow non-state participants and if the rival state accepts a name. Taiwan's economy and its 23 million people are why others bother. A new small project would have no such weight, although the technique of negotiating a neutral name remains available in principle.
chinese-taipei-formula.why: Left out the 1981 Lausanne Agreement, which is the actual settlement, and the 2018 referendum.

liberty-dollar.story:
The Liberty Dollar was a private coin. Bernard von NotHaus minted metal coins and offered them as an alternative to government money. His organisations, NORFED and Liberty Services, began exchanging Liberty Dollars for Federal Reserve notes in 1998, and federal agents raided the Evansville, Indiana, office in 2007, seizing documents, gold and silver. It stands as the main modern example of what can happen when someone offers a private currency to the general public inside a strong state.

On 18 March 2011 a federal jury sitting in Statesville, in the Western District of North Carolina, convicted von NotHaus, then 67. According to the FBI's release, the convictions covered making coins resembling US coins, issuing, selling, possessing and passing Liberty Dollar coins, passing coins intended for use as current money, and conspiracy against the United States. The coins had a current value of about $7 million, and the government sought forfeiture of about 16,000 pounds of coins and precious metals.

The same release said it is a federal violation to create private coin or currency systems to compete with the official coinage. US Attorney Anne Tompkins said that attempts to undermine the legitimate currency of the country are a unique form of domestic terrorism. On 2 December 2014 US District Judge Richard L. Voorhees sentenced him to three years of probation on each of three counts, served concurrently, plus six months of house arrest. He had faced more than 20 years in federal prison. The case was about physical coins that resembled US money, so it does not by itself answer questions about digital tokens with no such resemblance.
liberty-dollar.why: The sentence was vague and hedged and is now exact. The entry started at the 2011 conviction though the coins date from 1998, so the start is corrected and the 2007 raid added.

gambia-2014-coup-neutrality.story:
On 30 December 2014 gunfire broke out in Banjul, the capital of The Gambia. A small group led by Lieutenant Colonel Lamin Sanneh, a former commander of President Yahya Jammeh's guard, and Njaga Jagne, a Gambian-American captain in the Kentucky National Guard, tried to overthrow the president while he was abroad. It failed, and four people died, including Sanneh and Jagne. Jammeh returned the next day. In April 2017, after his government had fallen, police found the bodies of three alleged conspirators, Sanneh, Alagie Nyass and Jagne.

The plot was prepared largely in the United States. Cherno Nije, a developer in Texas, put up the money, with an initial budget of $200,000 and a later figure of $221,000. Banka Manneh in Georgia made introductions, and Papa Faal and Alagie Barrow helped with recruits and buying weapons. FBI raids began on 1 January 2015 in Georgia, Kentucky, Minnesota and Texas.

Those men were charged under a modern form of the Neutrality Act of 1794, now 18 U.S.C. § 960, which makes it a crime within the United States to begin, prepare, fund or take part in a military expedition against a country at peace with the United States. Faal, Barrow and Manneh pleaded guilty. Nije received a year and a day, Barrow and Manneh six months each, and Faal time served.

The case shows how the law reaches a private armed attempt at the point of departure.
gambia-2014-coup-neutrality.why: Added the 2017 discovery of the bodies.

adiz-high-seas.story:
An air defense identification zone, usually shortened to ADIZ, is a stretch of sky in which a country, by its own declaration, requires aircraft to identify themselves and report where they are going. The zone may run far beyond that country's own airspace, which ends at the edge of its territorial sea, the coastal belt it fully controls. Beyond that belt is international airspace, where the 1982 law of the sea treaty gives every country freedom to fly. The purpose is time. A fast aircraft crosses a 12-mile belt in moments, so a government that wants warning has to ask questions earlier.

The United States created the first zone on 27 December 1950, during the Korean War, out of fear of a Soviet bomber attack. Under its law no one could fly in the zone without filing a flight plan, and foreign civil pilots heading for the country had to report their position one to two hours out. If radio questioning failed to identify an aircraft, the Air Force sent fighters to take a look. Canada's rules of 1951 went further and warned of interception. About 20 countries and regions now have such zones, including India, Japan, Australia and the United Kingdom.

No treaty creates them. They rest on each country's own rule and on what others tolerate. The American position is that the legal basis is a country's right to set reasonable conditions of entry to its territory, so it applies its zone to aircraft intending to enter American airspace and does not require flight plans from foreign military or state aircraft that do not enter. The federal rule, 14 CFR Part 99, is not limited to commercial flying. It covers all aircraft except those of the Department of Defense and law enforcement, and it says that no person may operate an aircraft into, within or from a departure point within a zone without filing a flight plan. It has exceptions, such as flights that stay within 10 nautical miles of where they took off. Robert Beckman of the National University of Singapore noted in 2014 that global conventions do not expressly forbid the zones, while freedom of overflight remains the overriding rule, and that many countries appear to apply their rules to any aircraft passing through. One view among legal writers is that declaring a zone breaks no law. Another says the zones conflict with freedom of navigation.

The sharpest test came on 23 November 2013, when China declared a zone over the East China Sea. It imposed reporting duties on aircraft and covered islands Japan controls. Zones usually avoid disputed territory and mostly do not overlap, though Taiwan's has overlapped Japan's since Japan extended its zone near Yonaguni in June 2010. Japan warned of unpredictable events and the United States objected. In December 2013 South Korea expanded its own zone so that it partly overlapped those of China and Japan. China's zone is still declared.

For anyone thinking of a floating or flying settlement, the point is practical. Open-ocean sky is not owned by any country, yet a platform there may still find a nearby government asking it to report, and sending fighters to look when it does not. Such a zone gives the declaring country no ownership of the air. It shows how far a country can reach in practice without any new law.

add_sources.t: 14 CFR Part 99, Security Control of Air Traffic (text at ChanRobles)

adiz-high-seas.why: 'Commercial aircraft' was too narrow. 14 CFR 99.1 and 99.11 cover all aircraft except DoD and law enforcement. Also qualified the claim that zones do not overlap.
